body_markdown:
Race cars have a relatively finite lifespan. Once a chassis is no longer competitive, it often faces one of three fates: Evolution through modification, being torn down for parts, or getting parked. The most historic often get the last and most cruel option, only saved by the right owner who invests the time and effort to not only restore a retired racer, but keep it track-worthy. This C5-R is one of the lucky cars that gets to keep on driving.


Race cars live a tough life, and unlike with collector street cars, originality isn’t a primary concern. At least in higher levels of motorsport, however, the changes made to cars are often well-documented. Get enough businesses involved, and things start to get recorded for accountability’s sake. George Krauss is no stranger to digging through those records.


Krauss is one of the wild ones who likes to buy old race cars and get them back on track. While his day job might be landscaping, it’s historic sports cars that keep his world green. This Pratt Miller (formerly known as Pratt & Miller) C5-R is one he had his eyes on for a while before the right opportunity came up. Once he had the car,[the real fun began](https://youtu.be/eoBMmSzgbdM?si=Q_Kam5Mb0K97LCVX) : A full restoration to the exact condition it was in when it won the American Le Mans Series GTS championship.


C5-R chassis number 009 debuted at the 2003 24 Hours of Le Mans. For the whole 2003 season, this car and its sister car, chassis 008, were in for battle after battle with the Prodrive[Ferrari 550](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-550-maranello-laid-the-groundwork-for-ferraris-next-30-years/) s, though the primary fight was between the newer, faster Michelin tires worn by the Ferraris and the older rubber found on the Corvettes. The slower tire forced Corvette Racing to lean on strategy and pit efficiency to compete, and the team executed to near perfection. Chassis 009 won the championship, co-driven by Ron Fellows and Johnny O’Connell, and now wears the same livery to be locked in time at its peak.


This C5-R might be a retired race car these days, but even in retirement it has plenty of speed and continues to collect trophies in vintage races and events. Not all race cars are so lucky as to have a life of championships and loving owners well into retirement. This one not only deserves it but seems to be thriving. As it should.
